title: SWE-Bench ProMax: Refactoring as the Harder Coding Test
hook: Coding benchmarks keep saturating and keep turning out to be broken. ProMax swaps bug-fixing for multi-file refactoring — and the best frontier model still only solves 41.2%.
key_points: An audit cited by the authors found nearly 60% of unsolved SWE-bench Verified instances have flawed tests — too narrow (rejecting correct fixes) or too broad (checking unstated requirements).
Frontier models can also reproduce SWE-bench gold patches verbatim, suggesting the tasks leaked into training data.
ProMax uses refactoring instead: coordinated, behavior-preserving edits across many files, which is much harder to memorize.
170 expert-curated instances from real commits in seven languages — Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++, Rust.
Issue descriptions were rewritten from scratch and test suites hand-reviewed; tasks average 11.4 modified files and 261.6 changed lines.
Best frontier model under two agent scaffolds resolves only 41.2%, so the benchmark is far from saturated.
content_html: Coding benchmarks are decaying faster than the field can replace them. The team behind SWE-Bench ProMax cites an audit finding that nearly 60% of unsolved SWE-bench Verified instances have flawed tests — some too narrow to accept a correct fix, some so broad they check requirements the issue never stated — and notes that frontier models can reproduce gold patches verbatim, a strong hint the tasks are in their training data.
extra_html:
Their answer is to change the task rather than patch the old one. ProMax is built on code refactoring: behavior-preserving changes that have to stay coordinated across many files, which is both a more realistic picture of engineering work and far harder to solve from memory. The benchmark has 170 expert-curated instances drawn from real commits in Python, Java, TypeScript, Go, C, C++ and Rust. Issue descriptions were rewritten from scratch for precision, test suites were reviewed by hand to strip the narrow and broad cases, and small or single-file tasks were filtered out — leaving instances averaging 11.4 modified files and 261.6 lines.

The headline result is the useful one: under two different agent scaffolds, the best frontier model resolves just 41.2%. Shi et al., August 2026; the dataset is on Hugging Face.

prereqs.hook: Test a coding agent on real GitHub issues with real test suites - not toy problems - and the bar turns out to be much harder than HumanEval suggested.

flashcards.prompt: Why did the ProMax authors pick refactoring rather than bug-fixing tasks?
flashcards.back_html: Refactoring demands coordinated, behavior-preserving changes across many files — a harder, more realistic test of agent capability, and much less amenable to reproducing a memorized gold patch.

flashcards.prompt: What two opposite test-quality failures did the cited SWE-bench Verified audit find?

choices.text: Overly narrow tests that reject correct solutions, and overly broad tests that check unstated requirements
Tests that time out, and tests that depend on network access
Tests written in the wrong language, and tests with no assertions

flashcards.explanation_html: Both directions corrupt the score: narrow tests punish valid fixes, broad tests demand behavior the issue never asked for. ProMax's curation targets exactly these.

flashcards.prompt: Roughly how large is a typical SWE-Bench ProMax task?
flashcards.back_html: About 11.4 modified files and 261.6 changed lines per instance — substantially bigger than the tasks in existing coding benchmarks.
